desc:
On an old phone keypad each digit from 2 to 9 carries letters: 2: abc, 3: def, 4: ghi, 5: jkl, 6: mno, 7: pqrs, 8: tuv, 9: wxyz.

Pressing each digit of digits once and choosing one of its letters gives a word. List all such words in alphabetical order and return the k-th one (counting from 1).

Example: for digits = "23" the words are ad, ae, af, bd, be, bf, cd, ce, cf, so k = 5 gives "be".
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ the number of possible words
hints: Generating all words and picking the k-th works because there are at most 4<sup>8</sup> = 65,536 of them. Can you jump straight to the answer?
Because the letters of every key are in alphabetical order, the words appear in the same order as the numbers written in a mixed-radix system, where digit d has as many symbols as it has letters.
Subtract 1 from k and peel off letters from the right: k % len(letters) is the letter index of the last key, then divide k by that length and continue with the previous key.
editorial: Alphabetical order of the words is the same as odometer order: the last key changes fastest. So the (k-1)-th word, with counting from 0, is simply the representation of k-1 in a number system whose position values are the letter counts of the keys (3, 4, ...).

Take the last key, split off k % len(letters) as its letter and replace k by k // len(letters); repeat for the previous keys. This costs O(n) instead of enumerating up to 4n words, which is the same idea as 'jumping over' whole subtrees of a backtracking tree.
